stories.headline: Russian missiles and a drone fall in Poland during military exercises as Moscow pounds Ukraine

sources.body: Moscow pounded Ukraine with massive strikes Friday, with Kyiv saying at least six people were killed in the capital, and neighbouring Poland reporting two Russian missiles likely landed in the south-east corner of the NATO country, accusing Moscow of a "provocation." Hours earlier, Russia's Vladimir Putin vowed a "painful" response to Kyiv's strikes on Moscow's Crimea bridge after holding a summit with China's Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. FRANCE 24's Gulliver Cragg reports from Kyiv, Ukraine.
sources.headline: Russia pummels Ukraine with massive strikes, missile hits Poland

stories.headline: UK and EU agree to ease food-trade checks, link carbon markets and establish youth mobility

sources.body: Britain and the European Union agreed deals on trade, carbon emissions and youth movement on Friday, and pledged to rebuild ties with an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship. In a joint statement after a summit in Brussels, the UK and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap checks on the trade in plant and animal products, link their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other's countries for up to three years. FRANCE 24's International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani tells us more.
sources.headline: Burnham hails 'landmark' EU-UK deal as 'good day' for Britain, Europe

sources.body:
El primer ministro de Reino Unido, Andy Burnham, charla con el presidente del Consejo Europeo, António Costa, y la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, tras la segunda cumbre UE-Reino Unido desde el Brexit. / HANNAH MCKAY / DPA

El Reino Unido y la Unión Europea (UE) han llegado este viernes a un acuerdo que abre una nueva senda en las relaciones entre Londres y el bloque comunitario después de la traumática salida. Estas son las principales claves del pacto anunciado por el primer ministro británico, Andy Burnham; la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, y el del Consejo Europeo, António Costa:

Desde el Brexit , el programa de movilidad juvenil había constituido una de las grandes ambiciones de la UE. Llevaba años en negociación y España había sido uno de los países que más había presionado por su consecución. El paquete permitirá a los jóvenes comunitarios de entre 18 y 31 años (un año más de la edad tope inicialmente barajada, 30) trabajar, estudiar o viajar en el Reino Unido durante tres años , y viceversa.

En la práctica, 100.000 británicos y 100.000 europeos podrán participar cada año de una apuesta que aspira a eliminar barreras para las nuevas generaciones, tras el impacto que el fin de la libertad de movimiento ha supuesto para las perspectivas de la juventud de ambos territorios.

La cifra para los ciudadanos de la UE se establecerá en función de la población de cada uno de los estados miembro, mientras que los británicos deberán solicitar, al menos en un principio, un país concreto al que quieran viajar. Posteriormente tendrán la oportunidad de cambiar, con un total de tres destinos, si bien deberán pasar al menos 12 meses en un país antes de mudarse a otro.

Crucialmente para el Reino Unido, el acuerdo impide a ambas partes solicitar prestaciones sociales , o llevarse a personas dependientes como parte del programa, por ejemplo, un hijo.

Asimismo, la solicitud impondrá también el pago de una tasa de gestión y quienes deseen tomar parte en el programa tendrán que demostrar, adicionalmente, que cuentan con los fondos económicos necesarios para mantenerse durante su estadía en el extranjero.

El Brexit impuso barreras en agricultura y alimentos , con más controles y burocracia . Como resultado, las exportaciones británicas han caído un 32,5% desde 2019, una tendencia que el acuerdo sanitario y fitosanitario aspira a revertir con la creación de un área común , que eliminará la mayoría de los controles fronterizos, a cambio de que el Reino Unido adopte las normas de la UE.

Como resultado, el intercambio comercial será más sencillo y económico. Se prevé que esté en vigor en marzo de 2028, cuando dejarán de ser necesarios, entre otros requerimientos, los llamados certificados de salud, ahorrando a las empresas británicas el equivalente a unos 240 euros por documento. Se abolirán, además, los controles de productos lácteos, pesqueros y cárnicos, y se reabrirá el mercado comunitario a bienes británicos como salchichas, hamburguesas o moluscos.
sources.headline: Movilidad juvenil, eliminación de controles de alimentos e intercambio de emisiones: las claves del nuevo acuerdo UE-Reino Unido

stories.headline: AI sell-off erases Nasdaq's 2026 gains as Anthropic falls on its second trading day

sources.body:
The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning
sources.headline: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading

sources.body:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
sources.headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide

stories.headline: Trump threatens penalties and a possible ban on US companies building AI data centers abroad

sources.body:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
sources.headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

sources.body:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
sources.headline: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad

stories.headline: French parliament passes law giving police a presumption of self-defense when using firearms

sources.body: French senators gave final approval on Friday to controversial legislation granting police officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when using firearms, fulfilling a long-standing demand of the far right even as weeks of student-led protests have thrust the issue of police brutality back into the spotlight. Left-wing lawmakers have vowed to challenge the bill before France's Constitutional Council.
sources.headline: 'Licence to kill': French parliament adopts police shootings law slammed by activists

sources.body:
Detención de un manifestante por las fuerzas antidisturbios, el pasado 14 de noviembre, durante una protesta en Nantes 

El Senado francés ha aprobado este viernes, de modo definitivo y tras muchas horas de debate, una polémica proposición de ley sobre “la presunción de legítima defensa” destinada a que, en la práctica, la policía pueda disparar sus armas de fuego con menos reparos que hasta ahora.

La iniciativa legislativa, que tuvo ya la luz verde de la Asamblea Nacional hace meses, salió adelante con comodidad, por 205 votos a favor y 110 en contra, sin que se aceptase ninguna enmienda.

La medida, reclamada con insistencia desde hace años por los sindicatos policiales como parte de su autoprotección ante las violentas agresiones que sufren durante las manifestaciones de protesta o en otras situaciones peligrosas, fue defendida por el ministro del Interior, Laurent Nuñez, y respaldada por parte del centro macronista, Los Republicanos (LR, derecha tradicional) y el Reagrupamiento Nacional (RN, extrema derecha).

Los contrarios a la ley llegan a sostener que se trata de “un permiso para matar” y recuerdan que las fuerzas del orden francesas son ya las más letales de Europa y que se dan cada año demasiados casos de personas que mueren por no respetar controles policiales. Por esta razón anunciaron un recurso al Consejo Constitucional.

Tanto el ministro Nuñez como los defensores de la ley insistieron en que solo se ha hecho una pequeña modificación a la norma vigente y que, en realidad, los criterios para disparar siguen siendo los mismos, solo cuando la vida del agente esté en peligro y actuando con proporcionalidad. Lo que cambia es que cuando el disparo policial provoca heridos o muertos, no habrá, como ahora, una investigación penal inmediata, con interrogatorio preventivo al policía como si fuera sospechoso de mala conducta o incluso de homicidio, sino que la justicia se activará después de una denuncia de la víctima o de sus familiares.

Las asociaciones de defensa de los derechos humanos estiman que el establecimiento de la presunción de legítima defensa para policías y gendarmes y la no investigación penal automática suponen un riesgo para la sociedad. Creen que el lapsus de tiempo hasta que haya la denuncia puede permitir al policía construir una coartada o argumentos exculpatorios con la ayuda de sus compañeros presentes en el incidente. Los sindicatos policiales, por el contrario, se quejan de la indefensión que sufren los agentes, que resultan heridos por decenas o incluso centenares en las grandes jornadas de protesta, llegándose al extremo de que hasta en situaciones de mucho peligro dudan en desenfundar el arma porque son conscientes de las consecuencias que tendrá para ellos.

Corresponsal de 'La Vanguardia' en París desde el 2018. Anteriormente fue corresponsal en Alemania (1994-2002), en Estados Unidos (2002-2009) y en Italia y ante el Vaticano (2009-2018)
sources.headline: La policía francesa tendrá menos restricciones para poder disparar

stories.headline: Judge approves $7.25 billion settlement for Roundup cancer claims

sources.body:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits ⁠alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".

Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.

The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.

The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.

The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.

Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.

Some attorneys had objected to the settlement funds, arguing they were not enough, but the judge said he did not want to delay payouts to sick victims.

Bayer denies that its Roundup product causes cancer.

The settlement comes after the Supreme Court in June ruled in favour of Bayer, overturning a $1.25m settlement for a Missouri man who said Roundup and its ingredient glyphosate was to blame for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The court ruled 7-2, saying Bayer cannot be sued in state courts because federal regulations do not mandate a cancer warning label.

The company has faced thousands of claims in US state and federal courts from people alleging they developed cancer after using the product.

Roundup was developed by Monsanto in the 1970s. Its active ingredient, glyphosate, was identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, a unit of the World Health Organization in 2015 as a probable human carcinogen.

Bayer and some other regulators, including the US Environmental Protection Agency, have disputed those findings.

But the issue has forced the company through years of costly litigation in the US, as juries in several states opt to award billions of dollars to users of the herbicide.
sources.headline: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims

stories.headline: Mamdani proposes delaying Rikers Island's closure from 2027 to 2032

sources.body: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan moves the deadline from 2027 to 2032 to allow time to build the borough-based jails slated to replace Rikers.
sources.headline: Mamdani proposes five-year extension to shutter notorious Rikers Island prison

sources.body:
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."

"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.

Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.
sources.headline: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032

stories.headline: Spain approves data-center rules as industry, Madrid and Aragón prepare legal challenges

sources.body:
El govern espanyol ha aprovat aquest divendres el reial decret llei que regula la instal·lació de centres de dades i, en concret, les condicions del seu consum energètic. Després de rebre més de 600 al·legacions , l'executiu va enviar-lo al Consell d'Estat, que el va avalar a principis de novembre.

La nova normativa busca la màxima eficiència energètica d'aquestes instal·lacions, que generen un fort rebuig a diferents llocs del món per la gran quantitat d'energia i aigua que necessiten per funcionar.

El nou text de la normativa inclou canvis significatius respecte als esborranys inicials i ofereix una flexibilització més gran en l'aplicació dels requisits d'energia neta. Una flexibilització que ha estat rebutjada de ple pel sector.

En la proposta original es requeria que cada centre de dades acredités, hora per hora, que el 80% de l'energia que consumia procedia de fonts renovables addicionals. Ara s'estableix una moratòria de cinc anys per arribar a aquest percentatge. Es farà de manera esglaonada, i d'entrada la cobertura seria d'un 60% fins al 2028 .

Com a contrapartida, Red Eléctrica podrà ordenar que els centres redueixin la seva càrrega energètica a 0 si les necessitats del sistema elèctric ho requereixen. Aquesta eina inclou la capacitat de desconnectar-les de la xarxa sense dret a cap mena d'indemnització econòmica per a les empreses afectades.

La indústria rebutja de ple aquesta mesura, ja que, segons expliquen, un centre de dades no es pot aturar ni desconnectar en cap moment. Per assegurar el funcionament, hauria de posar en marxa generadors que funcionen amb carburant.

Durant la roda de premsa posterior al Consell de Ministres, la vicepresidenta i ministra per a la Transició Ecològica, Sara Aagesen, ha detallat que fixaran criteris de màxima eficiència energètica, l'etiqueta A, però que també tindran en compte la "regió climàtica" per requisits concrets que afectin la refrigeració dels centres.

"No es el mateix clima el d'Andalusia que el de la regió mediterrània o el Cantàbric, i en funció de les regions climàtiques, les necessitats de consum d'energia per refrigeració seran diferents", ha expressat.

El text, però, recull algunes excepcions, com el projecte de la gigafactoria de Móra la Nova , impulsat pel govern espanyol i català, ja que es considera un projecte estratègic. Amb tot, des del govern afirmen que aquest és un projecte que, a més, neix seguint criteris de sostenibilitat.

Segons fonts del sector, que el mateix govern espanyol hagi hagut de preveure excepcions demostra que l'aplicació de la normativa faria inviables molts projectes. De fet, asseguren que ja s'han congelat alguns projectes a l'espera de com és el text definitiu.

Una altra novetat del text és que queden exempts també d'aquesta normativa els centres de dades de menys de 10 megawatts . Per al sector, és una bona notícia per als petits, però també afegeixen que la majoria de projectes estan per sobre d'aquesta potència.
sources.headline: El govern espanyol aprova el decret que regula la instal·lació dels centres de dades

sources.body:
Centros de datos en una imagen digital GETTY

La Asociación Española de Centros de Datos Spain DC ha anunciado que recurrirá judicialmente el real decreto-ley aprobado este viernes por el Consejo de Ministros, que les obliga a que el 80% de su consumo de energía sea renovable. Al sector, que pedirá la suspensión cautelar de la norma al considerar que les impone condiciones de imposible cumplimiento, se le suma un frente autonómico: los gobiernos de la Comunidad de Madrid y de Aragón, ambos del PP, también han avanzado acciones legales.

"Pone en riesgo la soberanía digital de España", ha afirmado el presidente de la patronal del sector, Emilio Díaz, sobre la decisión del Ejecutivo. La vicepresidenta tercera y ministra para la Transición Ecológica, Sara Aaegesen, ha defendido que se trata de evitar un impacto de 5.000 millones en la factura energética de los consumidores.

El Partido Popular ha prometido que derogará las exigencias si gobierna, por el riesgo de espantar a los inversores, mientras que Ecologistas en Acción ha celebrado el paso del Consejo de Ministros, aun con un "amplio margen" de mejora.

Spain DC estima que las inversiones potenciales "en riesgo" pueden alcanzar los 66.900 millones de euros hasta 2030, apoyadas en las ventajas competitivas de España para los centros de datos: la misma energía renovable, la conectividad internacional y el ecosistema empresarial.

"No están regulando nuestro futuro, están obligándonos a exportarlo”, ha dicho la directora ejecutiva de esta patronal de los centros de datos, Begoña Villacís (exvicealcaldesa en el Ayuntamiento de Madrid por Ciudadanos). Ha denunciado que se están poniendo "trabas" a las infraestructuras que hacen posible la soberanía digital, la inteligencia artificial y la reindustrialización de España. "Si esta regulación es tan necesaria y beneficiosa, ¿por qué el propio Gobierno se autoexcluye de cumplir exigencias en los proyectos que promueve?", cuestionó antes también esta semana.

La primera propuesta de real decreto-ley del Gobierno ya contenía la exigencia de que los centros de datos acrediten que cubran el 80% de su consumo total mediante el autoconsumo o la compra de electricidad renovable ubicada en España, pero, tras someterlo a audiencia pública, optó por flexibilizar los tiempos y las formas para su cumplimiento, por ejemplo, admitiendo el almacenamiento con baterías o la electricidad de plantas solares fotovoltaicas sin importar su fecha de construcción.

Aun así, el presidente aragonés, Jorge Azcón, ha sostenido este viernes que el planteamiento "va en contra" de los intereses de su territorio en materia de inversiones y empleo, y el consejero de Digitalización madrileño, Miguel López-Valverde , ha tildado el texto de "grave error" por imponer "exigencias desproporcionadas", crear "inseguridad jurídica" y "poner en riesgo" unas inversiones "fundamentales para el futuro económico y tecnológico" del país, según recoge Europa Press.

Por su parte, Ecologistas en Acción reclama una moratoria de los grandes centros de datos en Europa y ha organizado movilizaciones bajo el lema " Stop dirty data centers ", en español: "Basta de centros de datos contaminantes" o, literalmente, "sucios centros de datos".

stories.headline: Catalunya activates wind emergency alert ahead of strong gusts on Sunday

sources.body:
Palmeras agitadas por el viento en Barcelona. / David Zorrakino / Europa Press

Protecció Civil de la Generalitat ha activado este viernes en fase de alerta el Plan especial de emergencias por riesgo de viento en Catalunya (Vencat), que hasta ahora se encontraba en prealerta, ante la previsión de fuertes rachas el domingo que podrían alcanzar más de 72 km/h.

Protección Civil ha alertado en un comunicado de que, según el Servicio Meteorológico de Catalunya (SMC), el domingo, desde la madrugada hasta la noche, aumentará la intensidad del viento de componente oeste , con rachas que pueden superar los 72 km/h, y en el Pirineo es posible que el umbral de aviso se supere en las cotas altas.

Durante las primeras horas del domingo, el viento soplará con fuerza en la Selva y el Vallès Oriental y se irá extendiendo hacia el sur, afectando a las comarcas del litoral y prelitoral de Barcelona y del Camp de Tarragona. A lo largo del día, el episodio también afectará a comarcas de la Catalunya Central, el Penedès y sectores del Pirineo y Prepirineo .

Ante este episodio de fuertes vientos, Protecció Civil re comienda cerrar y asegurar puertas, ventanas y toldos, así como retirar las macetas y otros objetos de balcones y terrazas que el viento pueda derribar. En el exterior, recuerda que deben evitarse los parques, los jardines y las zonas boscosas, y mantenerse lejos de muros, andamios, grúas y otros elementos que puedan caer.
sources.headline: Catalunya activa la alerta de emergencias por viento ante la previsión de fuertes rachas este domingo
